reference.source: Task Force Criteria for ARVC; ESC/AHA cardiomyopathy guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
clinicalPearls: A genetic cardiomyopathy in which fibrofatty tissue progressively replaces right ventricular myocardium, predisposing to ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death
Typically presents in young adults with palpitations, syncope, or exertional ventricular arrhythmia, and is an important cause of sudden death in athletes
Most cases are autosomal dominant and caused by variants in desmosomal proteins, particularly plakophilin-2 (PKP2), desmoplakin, desmoglein-2 and desmocollin-2
The resting ECG may show T-wave inversion in the right precordial leads and an epsilon wave (a low-amplitude terminal QRS deflection)
Diagnosis uses the Task Force Criteria, combining imaging, ECG, arrhythmic, tissue and family/genetic categories into major and minor criteria
Cardiac MRI demonstrates right ventricular dilatation, regional wall-motion abnormalities and fibrofatty infiltration; left ventricular involvement is increasingly recognised
Management centres on arrhythmia risk reduction with exercise restriction, beta-blockers, antiarrhythmic drugs, catheter ablation and an implantable cardioverter defibrillator in high-risk patients
Intense endurance exercise accelerates disease progression, so activity counselling is a key part of care
reference.pathophysiology: ARVC is caused predominantly by variants in genes encoding desmosomal proteins that maintain mechanical junctions between cardiomyocytes. Impaired cell-cell adhesion, aggravated by mechanical stress such as vigorous exercise, leads to myocyte detachment and death, with progressive replacement of myocardium by fibrous and fatty tissue. This begins in the right ventricle but can extend to the left. The scarred, electrically heterogeneous myocardium forms re-entry circuits that generate ventricular arrhythmias, while progressive myocardial loss can cause right and eventually biventricular dysfunction.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic right ventricular outflow tract tachycardia
Dilated cardiomyopathy with predominant right ventricular involvement
Athlete's heart with physiological right ventricular remodelling
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG for right precordial T-wave inversion, epsilon waves and prolonged terminal activation
Signal-averaged ECG to detect late potentials
Cardiac MRI to assess right ventricular size, wall motion and fibrofatty infiltration
Echocardiography for right ventricular dilatation and regional dysfunction
Ambulatory monitoring and exercise testing to quantify ventricular arrhythmia
Genetic testing for desmosomal gene variants and cascade family screening
redFlags: Syncope or aborted sudden cardiac death, particularly during exertion
Sustained ventricular tachycardia of left bundle branch block morphology
Family history of premature sudden death or confirmed ARVC
reference.prognosis: The clinical course is variable; with risk stratification, exercise restriction and appropriate defibrillator therapy many patients do well, but the condition is progressive and carries an ongoing risk of life-threatening arrhythmia and, in advanced cases, heart failure.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the arrhythmia as benign idiopathic outflow tract tachycardia and missing the underlying cardiomyopathy
Confusing physiological athlete's heart remodelling with early ARVC
Permitting competitive or endurance exercise, which hastens disease progression
Relying on right ventricular imaging alone and overlooking left-dominant or biventricular variants
Underestimating arrhythmic risk in gene-positive relatives with subtle findings
references: Revised Task Force Criteria for the diagnosis of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
management: Restrict competitive and endurance exercise, which aggravates desmosomal injury and accelerates disease progression
Beta-blockers as first-line antiarrhythmic therapy, with sotalol or amiodarone added for ventricular arrhythmia
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for secondary prevention and for primary prevention in patients with high arrhythmic risk
Catheter ablation, frequently requiring an epicardial approach, for recurrent ventricular tachycardia
Guideline-directed heart failure therapy for progressive right or biventricular dysfunction
Surveillance with ECG, ambulatory monitoring, echocardiography and cardiac MRI to quantify arrhythmia and structural change
Offer genetic testing of desmosomal genes such as PKP2, desmoplakin, desmoglein-2 and desmocollin-2, with counselling and cascade screening of first-degree relatives
Refer for advanced heart failure evaluation and transplantation in end-stage disease
